intro/hello: Welcome to attention and spatial transformers.
intro/once: The captioning network of the last chapter looks at its image exactly once.
intro/squeeze: A conv net squeezes the picture into one vector, and the R N N writes every word from that one summary.
intro/dig: Horse, grass, sky: every word has to be dug out of the same few hundred numbers.
intro/better: This chapter's better idea: let the network choose where to look, and look somewhere new for every word.
intro/soft: We will meet two families of answers. Soft attention looks everywhere at once, but with weights.
intro/stn: Spatial transformers learn to crop, zoom and straighten their input, with a smooth warp.
intro/secret: Both share one secret. They make where to look a smooth function, so plain backprop can learn it.
bottleneck/trans: The same problem shows up in machine translation.
bottleneck/enc: The sequence to sequence models of twenty fourteen read the whole English sentence with one R N N...
bottleneck/hand: then hand its final state, one fixed size vector, to a second R N N that writes French.
bottleneck/size: A five word sentence and a fifty word sentence get exactly the same number of numbers.
bottleneck/worse: So long sentences come out noticeably worse.
bottleneck/keep: The fix is to keep the whole input around, as a set of vectors instead of one.
bottleneck/image: For a sentence, that is the encoder state after each word. For an image, the grid of conv features, one per region.
bottleneck/pick: Then, at every output step, the decoder picks out what it needs right now.
bottleneck/phone: Describing a photo over the phone, you do not memorize it, then talk with your eyes closed.
bottleneck/glance: You glance back before each phrase: the horse, then the grass, then the sky. Attention gives the network that glance.
scores/vgg: Show, Attend and Tell, from twenty fifteen, built this into a captioner. Run the image through a conv net, and stop at the last conv layer, where it is still a grid.
scores/L: Fourteen by fourteen locations, five hundred and twelve numbers each: one hundred and ninety six feature vectors, v one to v L, one per patch.
scores/toy: To keep it small enough to see, here is a real see-far ten image, cut into an eight by eight grid...
scores/five: with five hand-made numbers per cell: brightness, blueness, greenness, warmth, and texture.
scores/step: At every step, the R N N does three small things. First, it scores each location: how relevant is this patch to the next word?
scores/query: It turns its hidden state, h, into a query, a wish list of features. If the next word is sky, the wish is bright, blue, and smooth.
scores/dot: Each location is graded by a dot product: multiply its features by the query, entry by entry, and add up.
scores/match: Where features match the wish, the products are positive, and the score is high.
scores/clash: Where they clash, like the dark, textured horse, the score goes negative.
scores/map: Do that for all sixty four cells, and you get a map of scores. Purple is high, dark is low.
scores/nothing: Nothing is chosen yet: just one score per location, like the class scores of a linear classifier.
softmax/second: Second, the scores become a probability distribution over locations, with the same soft max used for class scores.
softmax/exp: To get there, exponentiate. e to the power of anything is positive, so even negative scores become small positive numbers.
softmax/win: And it grows fast: each extra point of score multiplies the result by about two point seven, so high scores win big.
softmax/max: Subtracting the top score first changes nothing, but keeps the numbers from overflowing.
softmax/norm: Then divide by the total. Each weight, alpha i, lands between zero and one, and together they sum to one.
softmax/budget: Think of it as a budget of attention, one hundred percent, spread over the image.
softmax/map: On the image, the bright cells get the attention. Most of the budget lands on a few patches of sky.
softmax/sharp: A sharpness knob, multiplying the scores, sets how peaked it is.
softmax/low: Turn it down, and the attention spreads out over everything.
softmax/high: Turn it up, and it locks onto a single cell.
context/third: Third, the network reads the image through those weights: a weighted average of the feature vectors.
context/scale: Scale each location's vector by its weight, and add them all up.
context/one: The result, z, is a single vector, the same size as one location's features.
context/mostly: But it mostly describes the high attention places. The gold bars come out bright, blue and smooth, close to the query.
context/color: Average the pixel colors with the same weights, and you get the pale blue of the sky.
context/expect: Another way to read this sum: as an expectation, a probability weighted average.
context/die: Roll a fair die, and the expectation is three and a half, even though no single roll is three and a half.
context/soft: Soft attention computes the expected feature vector directly, as if picking locations at random with probabilities alpha.
context/diff: Every step was a multiply, an add, or an exponential, so it is all differentiable, and backprop can tune it.
context/nolabel: No label ever has to say where to look.
loop/put: Put together, one time step of an attention captioner reads like this.
loop/init: Start from the grid of features, with a first hidden state computed from the image.
loop/att: Score every location against the hidden state, soft max, and average: that is the context, z.
loop/rnn: Feed z, along with the previous word, into the L S T M.
loop/two: Out come two things: a distribution over words, from which the next word is sampled...
loop/back: and a new hidden state, which goes back to score the locations again, for the step after.
loop/maps: In a trained model, the attention maps line up with the words, startlingly well.
loop/horse: While writing horse, the bright region sits on the horse. At the word grass, it moves down to the grass.
loop/nobody: Nobody labeled those regions. The model found that looking at grass helps predict the word grass.
loop/mistakes: The maps also make mistakes legible: when a caption goes wrong, you can often see where the model was looking.
hard/literal: The same paper tried a more literal version: instead of averaging, pick one location, and look only there.
hard/die: Treat the weights as a loaded, sixty four sided die, and use only the cell it lands on. That is cheaper, and arguably closer to how eyes work.
hard/nograd: But a random draw has no gradient. Nudge a weight, and the pick usually does not change at all...
hard/jump: or it suddenly jumps to another cell. There is nothing smooth for backprop to follow.
hard/rl: So hard attention is trained with tools from reinforcement learning, the re-inforce family.
hard/reinf: Sample a location, see how good the caption was, and make that choice more likely if it helped. It works, but noisily.
hard/picks: Now watch the picks pile up. Each single pick is noisy...
hard/converge: but their average, the teal marks, closes in on the gold bars. Soft attention is the expected value of hard attention.
hard/cost: Soft attention skips the noise by computing the expectation exactly. The price: it reads every location, every step.
translation/inspired: Soft attention for captioning was itself inspired by machine translation.
translation/bahdanau: In twenty fifteen, Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio let a translation decoder attend over the encoder states, one per source word.
translation/same: It is exactly the same three steps. Score each source word against the decoder's state...
translation/soft: soft max the scores into weights, and average the encoder states into a context for the next word.
translation/grid: Plot the weights as a grid, output words down, source words across, and you get a soft alignment.
translation/diag: It is mostly diagonal, since the two languages mostly keep the same order...
translation/swap: but it bends where they differ. Black cat becomes chat noir: the noun comes first in French, and the attention crosses over.
translation/split: And one French word, dor, spreads its attention over two English words: is sleeping.
translation/speech: The pattern spread to anything sequential: speech recognizers attend over audio frames, and video captioners over frames in time.
draw/limit: Attention over a fixed grid can only choose among its cells, at its resolution.
draw/any: Could a network attend to an arbitrary box, at any position, and any size?
draw/draw: DRAW, also from twenty fifteen, an R N N that paints step by step, reads through an N by N grid of Gaussian filters.
draw/nums: The R N N outputs just a few numbers. The grid's center, g X and g Y...
draw/stride: the stride, delta, how far apart the filters sit, which sets the zoom, and a blur, sigma.
draw/mu: The filter centers are N evenly spaced points around g X, delta pixels apart.
draw/bell: Each filter is a bell curve over the pixel columns: a pixel's weight falls off smoothly with distance from the center, and each row sums to one.
draw/read: Blur and sample the rows with F Y, and the columns with F X, and the image shrinks to a six by six glimpse.
draw/move: Move the center, and the glimpse slides across the image.
draw/zoom: Widen the stride to see the whole picture coarsely. Shrink it to zoom in on a detail.
draw/smooth: A crop and a zoom, built from smooth bell curves instead of hard edges, so the network gets a gradient for moving and resizing its window.
stn/jader: Spatial transformer networks, also from twenty fifteen, extend this to any smooth warp, in a layer for any conv net.
stn/in: It takes an input, U, an image or a feature map, and produces an output, V, in three parts.
stn/loc: First, a localization network, any small network, looks at U, and outputs the parameters, theta, of a transform.
stn/six: For an uh-fine transformation, any mix of zoom, rotation, shift and shear, that is just six numbers.
stn/gridgen: Second, a grid generator lays a regular grid over the output, and asks where in the input each output pixel should read from.
stn/matrix: That is one matrix multiply: theta, times the target position with a one stacked under it.
stn/bias: That one is the bias trick from linear classifiers: it lets the same multiply add the shift.
stn/sampler: Third, a sampler reads the input at those positions.
stn/identity: With theta equal to the identity, every pixel reads from its own position, and the layer does nothing.
stn/zoom: Halve the diagonal, and the grid covers only the middle of the input: a two times zoom.
stn/rotate: Rotate the grid, and the output turns the other way, because the grid says where to read, not where to write.
stn/shear: Shift it, shear it: the output is always that region, straightened out.
bilinear/frac: Source positions rarely land exactly on a pixel. Here the grid reads at x equals zero point six, y equals zero point three.
bilinear/four: So the sampler blends the four nearest pixels.
bilinear/area: Each neighbor's weight is the area of the rectangle opposite it. The closer the point is to a pixel, the bigger that pixel's rectangle.
bilinear/sum: The four rectangles tile one square, so the weights always sum to one.
bilinear/value: The output is the weighted sum of the four gray values.
bilinear/slide: Slide the point, and the value changes smoothly, with no jumps.
bilinear/grad: So it has a slope. The red arrow is the gradient of V with respect to the point's position: the way to make the output brighter.
bilinear/pix: That gives two gradients. One with respect to the pixel values, so earlier layers can learn...
bilinear/where: and one with respect to the sampling position, so the localization net learns where to look.
bilinear/kink: Strictly, the weights have kinks at whole pixels, where the gradient is only a sub-gradient. In practice, that does not matter.
learned/nolabel: Nothing ever tells the localization network which transformation is right.
learned/loss: It is trained only by the final loss. If straightening the input makes the classifier more accurate...
learned/push: then gradients flowing back through the sampler push theta toward straightening.
learned/mnist: On distorted em nist, with digits randomly rotated, scaled and shifted, often in clutter...
learned/undo: the transformer learned to undo the distortion, handing the classifier an upright, centered digit, and beat plain conv nets.
learned/svhn: On Street View house numbers, it cropped and straightened the digits, and improved accuracy.
learned/birds: On fine-grained bird species, a network with two transformers in parallel learned, with no part labels at all...
learned/head: to have one zoom in on the bird's head, and the other on its body.
learned/drop: Because it is differentiable, it drops in anywhere, at the input or between conv layers, and the network trains as usual.
outro/after: Then came a twist. In twenty seventeen, Attention Is All You Need asked: what if we drop the R N N, and keep only attention?
outro/every: In the Transformer, every position of a sequence attends to every other position.
outro/qkv: Each word computes a query, and every word offers a key and a value.
outro/same: Query key dot products give scores, a soft max gives weights, and each word becomes a weighted average of the values: this chapter's recipe, for every word at once.
outro/parallel: With no recurrence, it trains in parallel on G P Us. It took over translation, then nearly all of language.
outro/vit: Vision followed. The Vision Transformer cut images into sixteen by sixteen pixel patches, treated each as a word, and matched the best conv nets, given enough data.
outro/recap1: To recap: one summary vector is a bottleneck. Soft attention keeps a set of vectors, and at every step scores, soft maxes and averages them.
outro/recap2: Hard attention samples one location instead, and trains with reinforcement learning.
outro/recap3: Spatial transformers predict a warp, turn it into a sampling grid, and read it bilinearly, smooth in both pixels and positions.
outro/next: Next, video, and learning without labels: autoencoders, and networks that learn to make new images.
outro/dl26: And when you are ready, the D L twenty six course picks up from here, with transformers.
